subtitle: Intercultural development begins with understanding your own assumptions. From there, you will learn to respond across cultural differences and build a more thoughtful leadership practice.
scope: For leaders and supervisors across DHS. This optional course supports intercultural learning and practical leadership; it does not administer the IDI, infer anyone’s assessed orientation or establish a personnel score. Learning and formal employment responsibilities remain distinct. Use practice cases here and approved handling for actual information. Staff retain responsibility for their work with consultant guidance when useful. Excluded Native American or Tribal-specific matters go to the appropriate office within ADSA (Aging and Disability Services Administration).
introTranscript: Intercultural development asks leaders to examine the habits they bring to an encounter as well as the differences they notice in others. A familiar meeting style, hiring example or feedback routine can feel neutral because it is familiar. Learning begins when we can describe that expectation, consider another meaning and choose a response that fits the people and the work. The Intercultural Development Continuum offers a way to understand increasing complexity in responding to cultural differences. It is a learning reference here, not an assessment of anyone completing this course. You will connect reflection and adaptive practice to hiring, onboarding, supervision, development and retention, while preserving actual authority and required responsibilities. The aim is growth in understanding and action, with honest evidence about what changed.

lessons.summary: Examine a familiar expectation before treating it as the only reasonable way to work.

intro.heading: Which expectations feel obvious to you?
intro.body:
A leader asks a group for immediate reactions to a complicated proposal. Two people speak quickly. One asks for time to read the figures, and another sends a useful question later. The leader concludes that the first two are engaged and the others lack confidence. That conclusion goes beyond the evidence. The different responses could reflect available information, responsibility for accuracy, familiarity with the topic, language processing, an access issue, a learned communication expectation or several factors together. The leader’s own expectation about prompt public speaking also needs examination.

Culture includes shared meaning, values and ways of relating, alongside more visible practices. UNESCO’s broad definition is useful for understanding that culture is more than clothing, food or celebrations. Council of Europe educational material also describes variation within groups and a person’s participation in several cultural contexts. These resources do not tell you what a particular employee believes. They invite a more careful inquiry into meaning, including the assumptions that seem ordinary to you.

Start with a personal reflection that does not need to be shared. What did you learn about a good leader, a respectful disagreement or a convincing answer? In which settings did that expectation work well? What happens when a different setting requires something else? You might discover that you value decisive speech because it helped a past team act quickly. That experience can remain valuable while you recognize that an evidence review also needs time for careful questions. Development involves expanding understanding, rather than declaring your earlier experience worthless.

Separate observation from explanation. “Two participants asked to review the document after the meeting” describes what happened. “People from their background dislike responsibility” assigns a group explanation that the observation does not establish. The first statement gives you a work question: was the material available soon enough, was the decision question clear and did the response route allow useful review? The second can close the inquiry before you understand it, and may influence opportunities unfairly.

Consider your effect as a leader. Employees may adjust to your preferences even when the adjustment hides information you need. If you praise only rapid public answers, someone with an unresolved question may stay quiet rather than challenge your idea. That does not prove a cultural cause, but it is a reason to examine the invitation and your response. Ask what information would make the discussion useful. Avoid demanding an identity story or making one colleague explain an entire community.

The employee lifecycle provides concrete places to apply this reflection. During hiring, ask whether a preference for a familiar speaking style is being mistaken for a job requirement. During onboarding, explain the decision route instead of testing whether a new colleague already knows it. During supervision, distinguish the quality of the work from similarity to your own preferred presentation. Development and retention also depend on whether opportunities and feedback are understandable. These are questions to examine within the actual employment process, not permission to change selection rules or disregard established responsibilities.

You can begin with one expectation and one situation. Write what you observed, your initial explanation and an alternative that the evidence still allows. Then choose a neutral question or a practical clarification. Keep private personal reflection separate from actual personnel documentation. If a formal concern or access request arises, use its responsible route. A thoughtful reflection should make your next interaction more accurate and respectful; it should not become a private rating of someone else’s culture.

flashcards.back: Shared meanings, practices and expectations that people draw on in varied ways; no group description explains a whole individual.
An explanation or expectation that needs examination rather than being treated as established fact.
Learning to understand and respond to cultural similarities and differences with greater complexity.

Learning to understand an encounter through another cultural meaning, then changing your response appropriately. For example, reconsider direct challenge as the only sign of respect and offer a context-first way to question evidence. This does not assess anyone’s IDC orientation.
Examination of your own understanding and actions; it need not become a shared identity account or employee score.

items.title: An expectation with a history
items.body: A preference for fast spoken decisions may have helped you in an urgent operational setting. Naming that history makes the preference understandable without making it universal. A policy review may require slower evidence checking. Ask which feature of the current task matters, then decide whether the familiar approach still serves it. The learning question concerns your expectation and its effect, not whether one whole background is more suitable for leadership.

items.title: An observation with several explanations
items.body: A colleague’s later written question tells you that they raised a question later. It does not establish why. Earlier access to the draft, workload, language, role or a learned expectation could matter. You can check the practical review conditions without collecting a cultural profile. If the colleague voluntarily explains a personal connection, keep it within the situation they described rather than turning it into a rule for others.

items.title: A reflection that preserves responsibility
items.body: Personal reflection can help you notice what you value and how that affects choices. It does not waive a reporting duty, a selection criterion or an information restriction. A leader can ask a more careful question and still follow the responsible process. Keep speculative identity explanations out of employee records, and use the established route when the actual situation involves an employment or accommodation decision.

tabs.label: Familiar means effective
tabs.body: The leader treats immediate public speaking as the definition of engagement because that style is familiar. This can make quick participation visible while hiding careful analysis offered later. Before using the interpretation to assign opportunities, examine what the task requires and what each contribution adds. Familiarity is evidence about the leader’s experience, not proof that every other style is less useful.

tabs.label: Different means uncertain
tabs.body: The leader notices a different response and keeps the explanation open. This creates a useful question about information and timing rather than a personal judgment. The uncertainty is not a reason to ignore the work: the leader can clarify when questions are needed and how they will be considered. A practical response does not require certainty about the colleague’s culture.

tabs.label: Learn and respond
tabs.body: The leader examines their own preference, provides the approved draft earlier and explains the decision question. They then check whether useful evidence reaches the review. This approach connects reflection to action without promising that a format change solves every barrier. Personal learning and work improvement can both matter, and neither establishes an assessed intercultural orientation.

check.question: A leader receives a useful written question after a meeting and initially calls its author disengaged. What should the leader examine first?
check.correct: The actual contribution, the review conditions and their own expectation about immediate public answers.
wrong: Which cultural group can explain the employee’s attitude.
Whether delayed speaking proves the employee belongs in a lower developmental stage.
How to require every future answer to follow the leader’s preferred style.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response checks evidence and the leader’s assumption, while leaving room for a better explanation and a practical improvement.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A group explanation assumes a cause the observation does not establish. A delayed answer is not an IDI assessment or a basis for ranking. Requiring one preferred style preserves the unexamined expectation rather than testing whether it serves the task. Examine the contribution and conditions before making a judgment.

items.text: A question about missing figures arrived after the meeting.
People from this background never take initiative.
Why do I treat a rapid spoken answer as the main sign of engagement?
The approved draft was first shown during the meeting.
Silence proves a lower intercultural orientation.
Which review conditions would allow me to hear useful evidence?

lessons.objective: Describe the five IDC orientations as patterns of experiencing cultural difference.

A learning activity cannot place people on the continuum.

lessons.statement: Use the continuum to expand your questions and responses, not to place a colleague in a category.

image.caption: Leaders consider different ways to understand cultural similarities and differences.

intro.heading: What does the model help you understand?
intro.body:
The Intercultural Development Continuum, or IDC, describes increasing complexity in how cultural differences and similarities are experienced. The official IDI organization presents five orientations: Denial, Polarization, Minimization, Acceptance and Adaptation. These are developmental concepts, not job grades or rankings of human importance. This course uses them to examine possible patterns in reasoning and to develop a broader repertoire of responses. It does not provide an assessment or tell you where anyone is located.

Denial can miss or avoid cultural difference. In a learning example, a leader may not notice that a familiar interaction has different meanings for participants. Polarization organizes difference into an evaluative divide, such as treating one approach as inherently superior or inferior. Minimization highlights commonality in a way that may obscure meaningful differences. Acceptance recognizes and explores different cultural patterns. Adaptation involves a shift in perspective and behavior that can bridge difference appropriately. The official descriptions are more detailed than these brief teaching summaries, and they should not be reduced to a single phrase someone says.

A common purpose can be useful at every point in a discussion. The difficulty is assuming that common purpose makes every experience interchangeable. A leader might say, “We all want a successful onboarding experience, so there is no need to ask how the instructions work for different people.” The first part can support collaboration; the conclusion closes inquiry. A more thoughtful response preserves the shared purpose and asks which parts of the onboarding route are actually understood and usable. Examining differences need not mean abandoning common ground.

Acceptance includes examining how a practice makes sense through different culturally learned meanings. In a practice example, June learned that openly challenging an argument expresses respect: the idea deserves serious debate. Rafael learned to establish relationship and context before disagreeing, so an abrupt challenge can seem to disregard the person. Recognizing these meanings is more than saying that everyone wants an accurate draft. Adaptation also changes the frame: June can understand respectful disagreement as care for both the relationship and the evidence, rather than measuring respect only through her familiar debating style. She can then state that shared purpose, offer context first and invite a supported objection through a suitable agreed route. The response retains honest challenge while making room for another meaning of respect. These are illustrative individual histories, not rules about a population or proof that either person has reached an assessed orientation. One course response cannot establish the broader pattern a formal assessment examines.

The IDI is a distinct assessment process. These practice cases, reflection notes and work measures cannot substitute for it. Do not assign an employee an orientation because of silence, an objection, a communication style, course completion or an identity. Do not turn an actual or inferred result into a personnel record, an access gate, an opportunity score or a hidden label. A supervisor can address actual conduct, performance and work expectations through their responsible processes without using an intercultural category to explain the employee.

In this program, Integration means the people a process affects help design it; the name comes from Bennett’s developmental model, where it describes identity across cultures. Keep that program use separate from the official IDC: Integration is not a sixth orientation in the current five-orientation model presented by the IDI organization. You can discuss who helps design a hiring or supervision process without changing the source or claiming a new assessed stage. Accurate terms help colleagues understand what the program teaches and what it does not measure.

Development is a continuing practice. A person can use a helpful question in one situation and struggle to understand a different encounter. Reflection can be uncomfortable without implying that the person is less valuable. Leaders can model the willingness to examine an assumption, seek appropriate feedback and try a different response. Use the continuum to ask how reasoning may narrow or expand the understanding of difference. Keep the person’s learning agency intact, and leave formal assessment to its separate responsible process.

items.title: Commonality and meaningful difference
items.body: A shared commitment to accurate service is useful common ground. It does not tell you whether every employee understands an instruction in the same way. A leader can preserve the goal and examine different meanings or barriers. This is a learning choice about inquiry, not a declaration that everyone who mentions a common goal is at Minimization. The context and the broader pattern matter, and this course does not assess them.

items.title: Understanding and adaptive action
items.body: Understanding that another person gives a different meaning to disagreement is valuable, but adaptation involves more than a softer message. A leader can question the culturally learned frame that equates public challenge with respect, consider a frame in which context and relationship are part of respectful disagreement, and choose a response that works across those meanings. In the June and Rafael example, that could mean stating a shared evidence-review purpose, establishing context and inviting an objection in an agreed sequence. The evidence still needs scrutiny; the route no longer assumes one familiar display of candor is the only honest one. A changed response can be examined without diagnosing the leader’s orientation or assigning Rafael a group preference.

items.title: An example and an assessment
items.body: A practice scenario is designed to teach a particular decision. Its limited facts cannot establish an actual employee’s developmental pattern. An IDI assessment belongs to its separate professional process. Keep course answers, reflection and operational results out of any informal orientation scoring. If you want evidence that an onboarding instruction became clearer, examine its usability rather than inventing an IDI result from the response.

tabs.heading: Compare how the model is used

tabs.label: A label for people
tabs.body: A leader calls a questioning employee Minimization and withholds a stretch assignment. This converts a developmental concept into an unsupported employment judgment. The label can hide whether the question identified a real evidence gap. Address the actual task and responsible selection process instead of guessing an orientation or using learning as an opportunity gate.

tabs.label: A lens for reasoning
tabs.body: A leader examines whether their explanation assumes that one common purpose makes every experience the same. This directs attention to the reasoning rather than an employee category. They can ask which differences affect the work and what evidence is needed. The inquiry may support development without claiming that it reveals a formal placement on the continuum.

tabs.label: A separate formal assessment
tabs.body: Where an IDI assessment is used, its interpretation and handling belong to the appropriate assessment process. The course does not administer, reproduce or shortcut it. A practical work check can still ask whether instructions were usable and concerns received a response. Keeping the purposes separate protects both learning and the credibility of operational evidence.

check.question: After an onboarding practice, a leader says all participants reached Adaptation. What is the accurate response?
check.correct: The activity can support learning and reveal a practical result, but it does not establish anyone’s assessed IDC orientation.
wrong: Every correct answer is equivalent to an IDI result.
Integration must be added as the official sixth IDC orientation.
People who ask questions should be recorded as less developed employees.
check.feedbackCorrect: This preserves both the value of the activity and the separate purpose of an assessment.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A correct course answer does not assess the broader developmental pattern. The current official IDC has five orientations; program Integration, where the people a process affects help design it, is a different use of the word. Recording questions as employee development labels invents a personnel judgment and can obscure useful inquiry. Describe the learning and work evidence without claiming an assessed stage.

sorting.heading: Recognize the use of the term

items.text: Acceptance describes recognition and exploration of cultural patterns.
The people a supervision process affects help design it.
One meeting proves every employee is at Adaptation.
Minimization can emphasize commonality while obscuring differences.
Following through on intercultural learning in onboarding.
A quiet employee must belong in Denial.

lessons.summary: Examine culturally learned meanings, change your frame and choose an appropriate response.
lessons.objective: Explain how two culturally learned meanings can change the interpretation of the same work exchange.
objectives: Explain how two culturally learned meanings can change the interpretation of the same work exchange.
Describe a shift from one familiar frame to a broader understanding without profiling a colleague.
Choose and review a response that bridges the meanings while preserving evidence, choice and legitimate requirements.
takeaways: A work behavior can carry different culturally learned meanings; ask rather than assume.
Adaptation connects a change in perspective to an appropriate change in response.

lessons.statement: Understand what the exchange means before deciding how to bridge it.

image.caption: Colleagues explore how respectful disagreement can take different forms.

intro.heading: From different meanings to a considered response
intro.body:
Practice DSD leader June invites new employee Rafael to challenge the evidence in a draft. June learned in family discussions, study groups and earlier work teams that direct debate shows respect. For her, questioning a claim openly says that the idea and its author deserve serious attention. She intends to welcome Rafael into the review. Rafael has learned in several relationships and work settings that a respectful disagreement begins by acknowledging the relationship and explaining context. To him, an abrupt challenge before that groundwork can sound like dismissing the person, even when the speaker intends a rigorous review. These are invented individual histories for this lesson. They are not claims about a nationality, race, language or every person who shares a background.

The same invitation now has two plausible meanings. June may interpret an immediate public objection as engaged honesty and a delayed question as avoidance. Rafael may interpret the invitation as uncertainty about whether careful relationship-building is welcome; he wants to question the evidence without treating a colleague as an opponent. Neither meaning can be inferred from a name, identity or silence. A draft might also be unclear, access could be missing or workload could interfere. Intercultural inquiry adds an examination of learned meaning; it does not turn every work difficulty into a cultural explanation or replace checking those other conditions.

Begin with June’s own frame. She could ask herself, “Why do I equate an immediate challenge with respect? What experiences taught me that sequence?” This is contrastive reflection: the leader notices the meaning she brings, then considers another meaning rather than treating her own as culturally neutral. Rafael’s account, in this practice case, helps her see that attention to relationship can support honest disagreement rather than hide it. The point is not to abandon candor or idealize the other approach. It is to recognize that candor does not have only one respectful form.

A neutral invitation can open inquiry without demanding a personal story. June might say, “I want us to test this evidence together while keeping the discussion respectful. What would make it easier to raise a concern, and how do you understand the way I invited the discussion?” Rafael may choose to describe what context-first disagreement means to him, answer only about the task or offer no personal explanation. He is not required to disclose family history or speak for a community. June can clarify the purpose and provide a usable response route regardless. In actual work, do not record speculative cultural explanations in personnel notes or copy a voluntary identity account into a learning exercise.

The change in frame is more important than an added polite sentence. June moves from “A respectful colleague challenges immediately in front of everyone” to “Respectful challenge can combine care for the relationship with scrutiny of the evidence; the sequence can vary.” She can now interpret Rafael’s request for context as a possible preparation for genuine disagreement, rather than automatically as reluctance to engage. This does not prove why every delayed objection occurs. It expands the interpretation she is willing to examine in this encounter.

Next, choose a fitting response. June states the common purpose, acknowledges the contribution Rafael brings and explains which draft questions remain open. She offers to begin with the decision context, invite the evidence concern and then discuss alternatives. They can agree on an authorized way to contribute before the review decision, including a written concern or a conversation where appropriate. A clear response point and owner preserve accountability. The arrangement must not hide contradictory evidence, promise Rafael’s preferred conclusion or let a leader bypass required review. June is changing how the review is conducted across meanings, while retaining the legitimate task.

Compare this with two shortcuts. Merely changing “challenge my draft” to “please challenge my draft” may improve tone while retaining the same narrow measure of respect. Guessing a cultural style from Rafael’s identity and performing it adds a stereotype, even if June means well. A third shortcut is to decide that relationship-first disagreement is always superior. That simply replaces one preferred approach with another. Effective adaptation requires an understanding checked in the particular encounter and a response whose appropriateness can be examined. Rafael may find public debate useful in a later situation; this account does not assign him a permanent communication category.

Check what happens. Can Rafael raise the evidence concern through the agreed route? Does June respond to its substance without treating its sequence as a lack of commitment? Do both understand the next decision and what remains unresolved? If Rafael brings a contradictory finding, the concern still needs a fair review. If no response arrives, the meaning and usefulness of the arrangement remain uncertain. June can reflect on whether she understood respect differently even before a work measure changes. A useful review result is not an IDI assessment or proof that either person achieved a permanent orientation.

Connect the practice to the employee lifecycle. In hiring, leaders can examine what they mean by confidence or initiative without changing approved criteria or supplying unequal coaching. In onboarding, they can make room for questions whose timing does not match a familiar public-speaking expectation. In supervision and development, they can consider how criticism, recognition or opportunity invitations carry different meanings and choose an appropriate response. In retention work, feedback about a relationship can inform inquiry without becoming a claim that an identity group prefers a particular style. These are ways to bring intercultural learning to real work, not permission to profile an applicant or employee.

Actual responsibilities remain. If the exchange includes a formal concern, managers and supervisors must follow the applicable immediate reporting route; an intercultural conversation is not a substitute. An access request belongs in its appropriate process. Information restrictions and decision authority still apply. Within those boundaries, a leader can understand the encounter more fully, change a response thoughtfully and continue learning without forcing anyone’s disclosure or ranking people by development.

lessons.keyStatement: A shift in perspective changes the meaning you consider, then informs how you respond.

items.title: Learned meaning is not a population rule
items.body: June’s direct-debate meaning and Rafael’s context-first meaning are facts supplied in this practice case. In actual work, you would not know them from a name or identity. A useful question invites a relevant account without asking someone to represent a community. Keep practical explanations such as access and workload open as well. If no personal account is offered, provide a clear review purpose and usable route anyway. Cultural understanding should expand inquiry rather than become another condition an employee must satisfy to participate.

items.title: A different frame, not only a different tone
items.body: June can move from treating immediate public challenge as the only sign of respect to understanding that relationship and evidence can both matter in disagreement. That wider frame makes a context-first question intelligible as possible honest engagement. Adding “please” does not necessarily produce that shift. Nor does declaring Rafael’s approach better than every other one. The leader examines why her familiar sequence feels right, considers another meaning and keeps the evidence open to scrutiny. This is a practice to reflect on, not an orientation assigned by the course.

items.title: An appropriate response with a real purpose
items.body: Having widened the frame, June can explain the review context, acknowledge the shared work and invite a supported concern through an agreed route before the decision. That connects perspective to behavior. The response should make it possible to challenge evidence, not require gratitude or guarantee agreement. Check whether the concern was heard and received a substantive response. If the route fails, revise it within actual authority. A positive intention, a friendly exchange or a completed worksheet cannot establish that the response worked.

tabs.heading: Compare the choices in this encounter

tabs.label: Change the tone only
tabs.body: June adds friendly words but still treats immediate public challenge as the only credible participation. Rafael receives a warmer message, yet the meaning that made the encounter difficult remains unexamined. Courtesy can help; it is not by itself the intercultural shift taught here. June should examine what she means by respect and invite relevant clarification, then consider a route that allows relationship context and honest evidence review to work together.

tabs.label: Assign a group style
tabs.body: June infers that everyone from a background prefers indirect disagreement and avoids asking Rafael about the actual exchange. This turns a possible learned meaning into a population profile and may erase his choices. Avoiding every challenge would also weaken the review. The practice account belongs to Rafael in this situation. Use it to understand the encounter, while leaving other explanations and future preferences open; do not use it as an identity-based rule for participation or opportunity.

tabs.label: Change the frame and response
tabs.body: June considers respect as care for both relationship and evidence, then establishes context and invites a supported objection through an agreed route. Her interpretation and conduct now connect: a context-first concern can count as genuine engagement. Check whether the concern was actually considered and whether both know the next step. The result can inform learning, but it does not certify either person’s IDC orientation or authorize a change to the underlying decision requirements.

check.question: In the practice case, what makes June’s response an intercultural practice rather than a courteous rewrite?
check.correct: She examines her learned meaning of respect, considers relationship-first disagreement as genuine engagement, then chooses and checks an appropriate way to review the evidence.
wrong: She adds “please” but still accepts only immediate public challenge as respectful participation.
She assigns Rafael a communication preference from his presumed group and uses it in every future interaction.
She treats relationship-first disagreement as universally superior and stops challenging the evidence.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response connects learned meaning, a broader frame and changed conduct. June retains the evidence review and checks the particular encounter; the course does not assess a developmental orientation.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A courteous word may help tone while leaving the same narrow meaning of respect intact. A presumed group preference profiles Rafael and ignores variation and his actual choices. Declaring one sequence universally better reverses the ranking and can abandon necessary scrutiny. Examine the meaning in this encounter, choose a response that bridges it and review whether the evidence can still be questioned appropriately.

sorting.heading: Connect the parts of the practice

items.text: June examines why she learned to hear immediate challenge as a sign of respect.
June considers relationship context and evidence scrutiny as compatible, then agrees a sequence for raising the concern.
June assigns every employee with a similar name Rafael’s supposed communication style.
Rafael may choose to explain the encounter, but a personal history is not required for a clear review route.
June checks whether the context-first route allowed the contradictory evidence to be heard and answered.
A polite message proves that both people reached an assessed Adaptation orientation.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: June welcomes Rafael into a draft review by asking him to challenge the evidence immediately in the team meeting. She learned to hear open debate as respectful candor. Rafael explains voluntarily that, in his own experience, establishing relationship and decision context first makes disagreement respectful. He has a contradictory finding and wants it considered before the draft decision. Neither person’s account establishes a group trait or an assessed orientation.
scenario.prompt: Which response connects a change in perspective to an appropriate review practice?
options: Keep the same public-challenge requirement and add friendlier words; treat a request for context as avoiding the work.
Record Rafael’s account as a permanent cultural preference for everyone from his assumed background.

Consider context and candor as compatible signs of respect, establish the decision context and agree a suitable route for the contradictory finding before the decision, then check its substantive response.
responses: The tone changes, but June still measures engagement only through her familiar meaning. The contradictory finding and another possible form of respectful disagreement may be missed.
The individual account becomes a stereotype and an unauthorized label. It does not explain every colleague or every future situation; no personal story should be required for a usable review route.

This broadens the meaning of respectful disagreement and changes the review practice accordingly. It preserves honest scrutiny, Rafael’s choice and the actual decision route, while checking whether the response helped.

lessons.transfer: Use a practice lifecycle encounter. Describe the observable exchange, your first learned meaning, another plausible meaning and how it would change your frame. Choose an authorized response and a check of whether it helped. Do not require a personal identity account or infer an IDC orientation.

move.control: You can examine the cultural meaning you bring, consider another perspective and choose an appropriate response while retaining legitimate duties.
move.failure: A communication adjustment leaves the original narrow frame intact, or a possible meaning becomes a permanent identity profile.
move.next: For one upcoming encounter, identify your own meaning of respect or participation, invite relevant clarification without requiring disclosure and consider how a broader understanding would change your response.

lessons.statement: Use intercultural understanding where opportunities, expectations and decisions are shaped.

image.caption: Leaders examine how work arrangements affect employee participation and opportunity.

intro.heading: Where does the expectation enter the decision?
intro.body:
Intercultural learning becomes concrete when leaders examine the arrangements through which employees enter, learn, contribute and develop. Hiring, onboarding, supervision, development and retention are connected, but they do not have identical authority or evidence requirements. A leader may control a routine invitation while a selection decision has an established process. The learning question is where a familiar expectation affects understanding or opportunity, and how it can be examined within the actual responsibilities that apply.

Begin with hiring. A practice panel prefers a candidate who answers quickly and uses familiar professional expressions. Another candidate provides clear evidence of the required skill in a less familiar style. The panel should examine the agreed job criteria and evidence, rather than equating familiarity with readiness. That does not mean ignoring communication requirements where they are genuinely relevant. It means defining and evaluating the actual requirement through the authorized process, without creating an identity-based preference or an informal intercultural score.

Onboarding offers a different decision. A unit tells new employees to “check with the usual person” before a submission. An experienced employee knows the route; a new employee does not. The leader can explain the contact role, required information and decision responsibility. This supports understanding without suggesting that the newcomer’s confusion is a cultural deficit. The formal approval still remains necessary. Clearer access to the route is the improvement, not the removal of the requirement.

Supervision asks leaders to distinguish work quality from similarity to their preferred style. In a practice case, two employees provide accurate analysis through different approved formats. A leader who praises only one presentation style may miss useful contributions or give unclear feedback. Discuss the actual task, evidence and effect. If a specific format is required, explain why and support its appropriate use. If more than one suitable approach is allowed, keep that choice visible rather than turning an unstated preference into a performance rule.

Employee development also needs transparent expectations. A stretch assignment may offer valuable experience, but “the person who seems ready” is not a clear account of how the opportunity is allocated. Use the actual selection criteria and responsible process. Make the work and its requirements understandable, then examine whether the invitation reaches eligible staff through an appropriate route. This course does not authorize a new promotion rule, a quota or a private cultural assessment. It helps leaders question where assumptions may hide the relevant evidence.

Retention should be examined through workplace culture, employee experiences and evidence rather than a single personal label. A colleague who stays may still face unclear opportunities. A colleague who leaves may have several reasons. Voluntary feedback can reveal a barrier within the scope of the account, but it does not represent every employee or prove a cause for all turnover. Use appropriate records and privacy protections, preserve uncertainty and involve the responsible office when the issue concerns a formal employment process.

Across these stages, ask a repeatable set of questions: what is the legitimate purpose, which expectation is built into the arrangement, what relevant evidence is available, whose perspective is missing and what can the responsible role change? Then choose a proportionate next step. A clarified invitation, a more explicit criterion or an approved feedback route can be useful without requiring a large new initiative. A larger policy question needs its appropriate analysis and decision process; a course activity is not a substitute.

Record the practical result separately from a developmental claim. More complete onboarding submissions can suggest that instructions improved, while the causal explanation may remain uncertain. A clearer opportunity invitation may improve access without proving that all inequity is eliminated. Personal reflection and organizational improvement both belong in intercultural learning, but the evidence for one should not be used to invent the other. Leaders can model growth by explaining what they learned, what they changed and what they still need to understand.

items.title: Hiring and onboarding
items.body: Selection needs the actual criteria and authorized process; onboarding needs a clear route to learn the work. A leader can examine whether a familiar style is being mistaken for skill, then explain the newcomer’s contact and approval route. These are different decisions with a shared inquiry into assumptions. Do not use a course response as a selection score or waive a required approval because an instruction was unclear.

items.title: Supervision and development
items.body: Feedback should identify the task, evidence and expected result. An opportunity should have understandable requirements and an appropriate selection route. If a leader favors a familiar presentation style, ask whether that preference serves the work or hides another effective approach. This is a reason to examine the decision with the responsible office, not permission to improvise promotion criteria or make identity the basis of the choice.

items.title: Retention and learning
items.body: A voluntary account can show that a particular employee found an opportunity route unclear. It is meaningful within that scope, but it does not establish everyone’s experience or the sole cause of departure. Examine appropriate evidence and possible influences. A leader can improve a route and review its use while keeping actual employee information in approved records and avoiding a private orientation or loyalty label.

tabs.label: A separate label for each stage
tabs.body: The leader calls a hiring concern bias, an onboarding concern culture and a development concern motivation without examining the arrangements. The labels can fragment a connected issue: unclear criteria and routes. A more useful inquiry asks what the decision requires and how staff can understand or contribute to it. Names alone do not identify the cause or the authorized response.

tabs.label: One rule for every stage
tabs.body: The leader applies a single informal method to hiring, feedback and promotion. This may seem consistent but can disregard different legal, contractual or agency responsibilities. A common learning inquiry can travel across the lifecycle; actual decision procedures cannot be assumed interchangeable. Confirm which role owns each decision and preserve the process that applies.

tabs.label: A connected, bounded inquiry
tabs.body: The leader uses the same questions about purpose, assumptions, evidence and missing perspectives, then adapts the response to each decision. A clearer onboarding instruction may be within local authority; a changed selection method may require another route. This connects development to real work while preserving the distinctions that make the action responsible and credible.

check.question: A leader wants to use intercultural learning to improve stretch-assignment access. What is a sound first step?
check.correct: Clarify the actual work and authorized selection process, then examine whether an unstated preference or unclear invitation hides relevant evidence.
wrong: Allocate opportunities by a guessed IDC orientation.
Replace the established selection process with an informal cultural preference.
Assume everyone who did not ask already has equal access and no concern.
check.feedbackCorrect: The inquiry connects a real opportunity to requirements, evidence and the responsible process without inventing a personnel rule.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A guessed orientation cannot become an opportunity score. An informal preference does not replace the actual selection authority or criteria. Nonresponse leaves questions about understanding and access; it does not establish equality or satisfaction. Examine the arrangement and use the appropriate process to improve it.

lessons.title: Seek feedback without making learning an employment label
lessons.summary: Use relevant feedback and private reflection while preserving formal responsibilities.
lessons.objective: Invite feedback about a leader’s action without requiring an identity account.
objectives: Invite feedback about a leader’s action without requiring an identity account.
Distinguish personal learning notes from actual employment and formal-concern records.
Identify when manager reporting or another responsible process must proceed alongside learning.
takeaways: Feedback should examine an action and its effect.
People can choose what personal reflection to share.
Learning does not postpone formal responsibilities.
lessons.statement: A leader can be open to learning and clear about their duties at the same time.

image.caption: A leader listens to a work concern and clarifies the next responsible step.

intro.heading: What are you asking the feedback to establish?
intro.body:
A leader wants to know whether a new discussion invitation is clearer. They ask each employee to provide a cultural identity story and a personal development stage. The request is larger than the work question and may discourage useful feedback. The leader needs information about the invitation: whether its purpose is understandable, how people can prepare and whether a relevant question receives a response. A personal account may add meaning if someone chooses to share it, but it should not be the required price of having the arrangement examined.

Frame the feedback around your action and its effect. “Which part of my invitation made preparation easier, and which part still needs clarification?” gives a specific subject. Explain what you can change and what remains required. Allow an appropriate way to respond, and be honest about how actual information will be handled. A promise of complete secrecy may be inaccurate where a manager has formal duties. A limited invitation with clear handling is more trustworthy than broad reassurance that cannot be kept.

Personal reflection has its own value. You may privately examine why a disagreement felt threatening or why you assumed a colleague would prefer a particular approach. That learning can deepen self-understanding even before it produces an operational measure. Do not require every employee to share the same private reflection or use the depth of disclosure as evidence of commitment. Staff can engage through the actual learning and work questions without supplying an identity narrative.

Keep records appropriate to their purpose. A practice course exercise can use invented names and details. Actual work decisions need their approved documentation and information-handling rules. Speculative cultural explanations and assessed or inferred IDI orientations should not become personnel data, opportunity scores or hidden categories. A responsible supervisor can document the actual work expectation, evidence and action without guessing that a developmental label explains the person. Where information handling is uncertain, use the appropriate agency guidance rather than copying sensitive material into a learning note.

Feedback can also reveal a formal concern. Under MMB Policy 1436, managers and supervisors must immediately report allegations or incidents of protected-class harassment or discrimination to agency HR or the affirmative action officer, following the applicable procedures. A learning conversation is not an informal investigation and cannot be a required step before reporting. Do not ask an employee to complete a reflection, reconcile with another person or wait for the next workshop before the duty is carried out. Respectful practical support can continue alongside the formal route.

An access or accommodation request similarly belongs to its responsible process. You can make an invitation clearer and examine whether a document is usable without requiring an identity story. But a general learning design does not automatically resolve every individual request or authorize you to disregard the current procedure. Use the route that applies, keep sensitive information within approved handling and avoid making the course a gate to assistance.

Seek feedback from more than one suitable source when the work calls for it. A colleague may explain the invitation’s clarity, an authorized process owner may explain a requirement and the consultant may help examine your reasoning. These contributions have different roles. The consultant provides guidance and feedback without replacing staff ownership of the work or a manager’s duty. One employee should not be made the permanent teacher or representative for a whole community.

Close the loop proportionately. Describe the change you made, the relevant feedback you considered and the limit of what it establishes. If you cannot make a requested change, explain the reason through the appropriate channel. You can acknowledge a mistake without making an unsupported admission about a formal case, and you can retain a legitimate requirement without dismissing someone’s account. The leadership practice is openness with responsibility: learn about your own effect, act within your role and follow the duties that remain.

lessons.keyStatement: A leader can be open to learning and clear about their duties at the same time.

items.title: Ask about the action
items.body: An invitation can ask whether your explanation of a decision made the next step understandable. It does not need a complete identity account or a guessed IDC placement. Keeping the subject specific can improve the feedback and reduce unnecessary disclosure. If someone volunteers a personal connection, respect its scope; do not assume that it represents every employee or authorizes storing the story in another record.

items.title: Explain handling honestly
items.body: People may need to know who will receive actual feedback and what happens if it raises a formal concern. Avoid promising absolute secrecy when your role has reporting duties. Use approved channels for real information and practice material for course practice. Privacy is not an excuse to ignore a duty, and a duty is not permission to circulate the account beyond the responsible process.

items.title: Act on a formal concern
items.body: If a manager hears an allegation within MMB Policy 1436, immediate reporting to HR or the affirmative action officer remains required. Do not investigate it through a learning group or make course completion the next condition. Appropriate support, clear communication and the formal route can proceed together. Cultural curiosity neither establishes the case nor removes the manager’s responsibility to act.

tabs.label: Compulsory personal disclosure
tabs.body: The leader requires employees to share an identity story to demonstrate engagement. This can burden participants and shift attention away from whether the leader’s action was useful. A quiet or private response is then misread as resistance. Invite feedback about the actual arrangement and leave personal reflection to the employee’s choice rather than treating disclosure as a performance measure.

tabs.label: Unlimited reassurance
tabs.body: The leader promises that everything said will remain entirely private, then receives an allegation that triggers a manager duty. The promise may conflict with what must happen next. Explain the relevant handling and formal route accurately before inviting real concerns. Trust rests on a responsible account of the process, not on a reassurance that the role cannot honor.

tabs.label: Relevant feedback and responsibility
tabs.body: The leader asks about the communication’s effect, offers an appropriate route and explains how actual concerns will be handled. They retain private reflection for learning and follow formal duties when needed. This keeps openness connected to the subject and protects the distinction between learning, work evidence and a responsible response to a formal concern.

check.question: A supervisor hears an allegation of protected-class discrimination during intercultural learning. What should happen?
check.correct: Immediately report it to agency HR or the affirmative action officer under the applicable policy, while keeping learning separate from the formal response.
wrong: Ask the employee to complete a reflection before taking further action.
Use the learning group to decide which cultural stage caused the allegation.
Promise secrecy and leave the matter entirely inside private learning notes.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response preserves the supervisor’s immediate reporting duty and avoids using a course to determine a formal case.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Reflection cannot become a gate before required reporting. A learning group cannot infer orientations or replace the formal inquiry. A secrecy promise and private note do not remove a manager’s duty under the policy. Respond respectfully, use the designated route and keep information within its proper handling.

items.text: Privately examine why a disagreement felt threatening to you.
Check whether the revised invitation explained the next step.
A supervisor immediately reports a covered discrimination allegation to HR or the affirmative action officer.
Consider another possible meaning without profiling a colleague.
Record the approved decision and the relevant reason in its proper work record.
Use the current responsible route for an actual accommodation request.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: At a practice leadership learning session, employee Tessa tells supervisor Malik that she experienced protected-class discrimination. Malik suggests a cultural reflection exercise and promises not to tell anyone until Tessa completes it. No formal report has been made.
options: Keep the reflection as the required first step.
Correct the handling explanation, immediately report through the responsible HR or affirmative action route and offer suitable practical support without an informal investigation.
Ask the group to assign both people an IDI orientation.
responses: The activity cannot delay or replace the reporting duty.
This preserves the required response while separating learning and practical support from a formal determination.
The course cannot assess orientations or use them to establish a discrimination case.

lessons.transfer: Draft a practice feedback invitation that names the action, asks about its effect and explains appropriate handling. Add the separate step for a formal concern.

move.control: You can invite useful feedback and reflect on your own effect while preserving actual information and manager duties.
move.failure: Learning becomes compulsory disclosure, a private employee label or a delay in a formal response.

lessons.title: Sustain development through practice and review
lessons.summary: Build a continuing plan that connects reflection, adaptive action and honest evidence.
lessons.objective: Write a development plan with a personal inquiry and a concrete leadership practice.
objectives: Write a development plan with a personal inquiry and a concrete leadership practice.
Choose a result check that fits the work without inferring an IDI score.
Revise an approach when evidence is missing or the proposed change does not help.
takeaways: Development continues beyond a course answer.
Personal reflection and practical action both deserve attention.
A result needs a limit and a next question.
lessons.statement: A continuing practice asks what you learned, what you changed and what still needs understanding.

image.caption: A group reviews an agreed action and considers what to learn next.

intro.heading: Build a plan you can actually use
intro.body:
A development plan should be specific enough to guide action and open enough to change as understanding grows. A statement such as “be more culturally competent” names an intention but leaves the next practice unclear. A leader can choose a personal inquiry, a work situation and a response to examine. For example: “I want to understand why I equate quick public agreement with a productive discussion. I will examine how I invite questions in one draft review, then check whether the relevant issues receive a response.” This connects reflection to a real interaction without making a claim about a formal orientation.

Begin with the inquiry. What expectation do you want to understand more deeply? It may concern disagreement, authority, relationship, time, communication or another meaningful aspect of your own experience. Reflection can remain private. You can examine it through appropriate learning resources, a voluntary conversation or consultant feedback, without making someone else responsible for explaining an entire community. A question about your own meaning should not turn into collecting colleagues’ personal histories.

Choose a concrete practice across the employee lifecycle. In hiring, examine whether you evaluate the actual agreed skill rather than a familiar expression. In onboarding, explain a decision route and check its usability. In supervision, clarify the difference between routine review and a formal process. In development, make the authorized opportunity requirements understandable. In retention work, keep a voluntary account properly scoped and examine possible influences. Start where your role has an actual responsibility and where a proportionate change is possible.

Compare the current arrangement and a proposed option. Explain how the option addresses the inquiry and what it requires. Sharing an approved draft earlier can create preparation time, but it needs permitted access and an owner. A new question route can invite useful evidence, but it needs a purpose and a response. Confirm the authority before acting. A leader’s interest in adaptive practice does not waive policy analysis, formal selection, reporting or information restrictions.

Set a result check that fits the practice. Was the instruction understandable? Did the relevant question reach the responsible person before the decision? Was the response explained? These checks can provide useful operational evidence. They cannot establish every employee’s satisfaction, a universal cultural change or a measured movement on the IDC. Personal learning may also include recognizing an assumption or becoming more comfortable with uncertainty. Describe that reflection in its own terms rather than forcing it into a numerical score.

Keep missing evidence visible. If only two people respond to an invitation, you know what those responses say; you do not know that everyone else agrees. If a revised process receives better questions, another change in workload or material may also have contributed. A bounded result can support the next action without claiming a single cause. Where the option did not help, examine why and consider a different response. Reverting or revising an approach can be responsible learning rather than failure.

Plan follow-through. Name who owns the work change, when its use will be reviewed and which decision remains open. The consultant can help test reasoning and provide feedback while staff and managers retain their tasks and duties. A learning partner can ask a helpful question without acting as an assessor. Avoid permanent dependence on one person to interpret every difference; build the capacity to ask, examine and act responsibly within your role.

Return to the broader purpose. Intercultural development can strengthen self-understanding, relationships and public-service decisions. It is not limited to producing a document, and it is not completed by declaring a stage. Leadership offers repeated chances to examine meaning and widen a response. A credible account says what you learned, what you did, what the evidence suggests and what remains uncertain. That combination gives the next inquiry a useful foundation without claiming that the work or the person is finished.

lessons.keyStatement: A continuing practice asks what you learned, what you changed and what still needs understanding.

items.title: An inquiry with personal meaning
items.body: A leader can examine why disagreement feels like a threat to authority and how that affects listening. The reflection has value even before a work measure changes. It need not be disclosed to the team or turned into a development stage. Use suitable resources and voluntary feedback, then consider a practical response that honors both your growing understanding and the responsibilities of the role.

items.title: An action with a legitimate purpose
items.body: A clearer onboarding route can make an approved process easier to understand. State the actual contact role, required information and next step, then confirm that the responsible office agrees with any change. The action does not remove approval or create a new entitlement. Adaptive practice is stronger when its purpose and authority are clear, because a helpful intention alone cannot authorize the arrangement.

items.title: A review that leaves room to learn
items.body: Check whether the revised route helped people complete the intended task and whether questions received a useful response. If information is missing, name the limit. If the result is disappointing, examine the design and conditions rather than assigning employees a resistance label. The next option may be different or smaller. Learning remains credible when revision and uncertainty are visible.

tabs.label: A broad declaration
tabs.body: The leader says everyone will reach Adaptation by the end of the quarter and treats completed courses as the evidence. This sets an unsupported assessment target and may encourage a score instead of reflection. A more useful plan names what the leader wants to understand and which actual practice will be examined. Course participation is learning evidence, not a measured orientation.

tabs.label: An action without inquiry
tabs.body: The leader adds another meeting format but never asks which assumption or barrier it addresses. The additional route may help, yet its purpose and effect remain unclear. Connect the option to a specific question about meaning or use, confirm the responsible authority and choose a proportionate check. More activity alone does not establish deeper understanding or better access.

tabs.label: Reflection, practice and review
tabs.body: The leader names a personal inquiry, an authorized change and a result question, then preserves what remains unknown. This allows personal growth and practical improvement to support one another without collapsing them into one score. Consultant feedback can refine the reasoning while staff retain the work. The plan is a continuing cycle of learning, action and review.

check.question: A revised practice onboarding instruction leads to fewer incomplete submissions. What should the leader conclude?
check.correct: The result may support a useful improvement in this route; examine other influences and remaining questions without claiming an IDI change.
wrong: Every employee has now reached Adaptation.
All employee experience barriers have been permanently removed.
Nonresponders must be satisfied because submission totals improved.
check.feedbackCorrect: The conclusion stays tied to the observed practice and leaves room for further evidence and personal learning.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A work measure does not assess IDC orientations. One improved route cannot establish permanent elimination of every barrier. Missing responses do not prove satisfaction, even when a submission measure improves. Describe the actual result, its limits and the next question rather than declaring a universal transformation.

items.text: Examine why I assume rapid agreement means understanding.
Clarify the approved onboarding contact and decision route.
The revised route coincided with fewer incomplete submissions; other influences remain possible.
Consider how my experience shapes the meaning I give to disagreement.
Assign a response owner and confirm permitted draft access.
Two respondents found the instruction clearer; other experiences remain unknown.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: A practice unit clarifies an onboarding submission route and sees fewer incomplete forms. move.control: You can sustain a learning practice and examine its effect without inventing an assessment or replacing staff ownership.
move.failure: A course becomes a universal success claim, or an action continues without a useful reason and review.

sources.title: IDI, LLC — Intercultural Development Continuum
sources.note: Describes the five official orientations: Denial, Polarization, Minimization, Acceptance and Adaptation. Course descriptions summarize concepts and do not administer an assessment. Integration refers here only to the program’s meaning: the people a process affects help design it.

sources.title: Council of Europe — Developing intercultural competence through education
sources.note: Educational reference for multiple cultural affiliations, variation, context and continuing learning, especially pages 13–17. A learning source rather than Minnesota employment authority; the course’s lifecycle inquiries and cases are authored examples.

sources.title: UNESCO — Universal Declaration on Cultural Diversity
sources.note: Broad concept of culture and the distinction between respect for difference and a justification for harm. This international declaration is not presented as a new DHS rule or a diagnosis of an individual.

sources.title: Minnesota DHS — Equity Policy
sources.note: Actual agency responsibilities and required equity-analysis routes remain in place. Optional intercultural learning does not authorize exemptions or automatically satisfy required training.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Harassment and Discrimination Prohibited Policy 1436
sources.note: Primary authority for immediate manager and supervisor reporting of protected-class harassment or discrimination allegations and incidents to agency HR or the affirmative action officer. Learning does not replace the formal response.

sources.title: Bennett, M. J. (1993). Towards Ethnorelativism: A Developmental Model of Intercultural Sensitivity.
sources.note: Source for the name Integration, which there describes identity across cultures. The meaning used in this program, that the people a process affects help design it, is the program’s own application. A licensed IDI assessment does not measure Integration.
